said: In June twenty twenty-two, prices in America were rising nine point one percent a year, the fastest in about forty years. Here is what that does to your money.
Ava had a plan. When she turned sixteen, she would use it to buy a new pair of headphones and a big pizza dinner with her friends.
Nobody stole her money. Nobody touched it. So what happened? By the end of this video, you'll know exactly where her money went, and how to protect yours.
Every month, government workers check the prices of thousands of things. Food, rent, gas, haircuts, car insurance, doctor visits.
Not everything in the cart counts equally. Rent and housing are the biggest part, about a third of the whole cart. Gas and food come after that.

said: If the cart costs one hundred dollars this year and one hundred and three dollars next year, inflation is three percent.
A little inflation is normal. The Federal Reserve actually aims for about two percent a year. Low and steady, so people can plan.
During the pandemic, factories closed and shipping got stuck. There were fewer things to buy. Cars, furniture, even computer chips ran short.
Ships waited for weeks outside ports in California, full of goods nobody could unload. Store shelves had gaps. Used car prices jumped by around forty percent in one year.

what: highlight "US Regular All Formulations Gas Price"
said: Then, in early twenty twenty-two, Russia invaded Ukraine. Oil, gas and food prices jumped around the world.
In early twenty twenty-one, inflation was under two percent. By June twenty twenty-two, it hit nine point one percent.
That was the highest rate since November nineteen eighty-one. A whole generation of Americans had never seen prices rise this fast.
Gas was the first thing people noticed. In June twenty twenty-two, the average price of regular gas passed five dollars a gallon for the first time.
Food at the grocery store rose about eleven percent in a single year, the fastest in more than four decades. Families started buying store brands and skipping meat.
Workers can lose too, if prices rise faster than their pay. In twenty twenty-two, many Americans got raises, but their raises didn't keep up.
Social Security is different. Its payments are adjusted every year for inflation. In twenty twenty-three, retirees got a raise of eight point seven percent, the largest in four decades.

said: Think of a family with a mortgage at three percent. Their payment stays the same, while their paychecks and their home value rise.
The Federal Reserve's main tool is interest rates. When inflation is too high, the Fed raises rates to cool things down.
Starting in March twenty twenty-two, the Fed raised rates eleven times, from near zero to above five percent. It was the fastest rise in about forty years.
It worked, slowly. Inflation fell back toward about three percent. But it came with costs. Mortgage rates more than doubled, and buying a home got much harder.
The Fed has done this before. In nineteen eighty-one, Fed chair Paul Volcker pushed rates near twenty percent to crush inflation. It worked, but it caused a painful recession.
Second, the government sells special savings bonds called I bonds, whose interest goes up with inflation. They're built for exactly Ava's problem.
Third, for money you won't need for many years, investing in a broad mix of companies has historically grown faster than inflation, though it can drop a lot along the way.
And if you work, ask for raises that at least match inflation. A raise of three percent when prices rise four percent is really a pay cut.
